one_liner: Rust single-node spatial SQL/DataFrame engine on DataFusion; beats DuckDB Spatial and GeoPandas on spatial and KNN joins.
what_it_does: SedonaDB is an analytical database engine (Apache Sedona subproject) that runs spatial SQL and DataFrame queries over GeoParquet, Parquet with WKB columns, Shapefile and GeoJSON, locally or straight from S3. You use it from Python (sd.sql(...), sd.read_parquet(...)), R, a CLI, Rust, or an ADBC driver; it does not offer a C++ geometry API. It replaces a query layer such as DuckDB Spatial or a GeoPandas script, not GEOS, CGAL or Boost.Geometry calls inside C++ code.
how_it_is_fast: Spatial joins are two-phase: a filter phase on a packed Hilbert-sorted R-tree (geo-index RTree<f32> over bounding boxes) and a refine phase that checks exact predicates with tidwall's TG library (y-stripes index, the default), GEOS or the Rust geo crate. A speculative execution mode samples the first 1,000 geometries and then decides whether to build prepared geometries on the build side, the probe side or neither. KNN joins have their own operator. The engine is columnar and vectorized on Arrow and DataFusion, runs multi-threaded with probe-side repartitioning, and can spatially partition and spill the build side to disk for joins larger than memory.
when_to_use: Spatial joins (point-in-polygon, intersects, ST_DWithin) and KNN joins over millions of rows in Parquet/GeoParquet on one machine: the largest wins on the page are q9-q12, where DuckDB 1.4.0 timed out or errored
Replacing single-threaded GeoPandas pipelines: SF1 queries ran 1.2x to 82x faster than a hand-written GeoPandas mirror, and SedonaDB finished SF10 queries where GeoPandas errored or timed out
Python or R analytics that already use Arrow, DuckDB or Polars and want a spatial engine with CRS tracking and zero-copy Arrow exchange
Joins bigger than RAM: the spatial join can partition the build side and spill it to disk
Optional GPU spatial joins (libgpuspatial, added in 0.4.0) for heavy joins, if you can build and run that path
when_not_to_use: Inside a C++ program that needs geometry predicates, overlays or an index: it is a Rust query engine, not a C++ library; use GEOS, TG or Boost.Geometry directly
Spatial aggregation queries: SpatialBench q5 ran 2.8x (SF1) and 3.5x (SF10) slower than DuckDB, and the project calls this a known weakness
Simple spatial filters where DuckDB Spatial is already in the stack: q1-q8 are roughly even (1.0-1.5x either way)
Projects that need a stable API: the engine is pre-1.0 (0.1.0 in September 2025, 0.4.1 in August 2026, workspace at 0.5.0) and adds features each release
Transactional or multi-node workloads: it is a single-node analytical engine; the project points to PostGIS-style databases and SedonaSpark/SedonaFlink for those

integration.dependencies: Python wheel (pip install "apache-sedona[db]" or sedonadb; conda-forge sedonadb); R package on R-multiverse; from source: Rust workspace on Apache Arrow 58 and DataFusion 54, with C libraries GEOS, TG, PROJ, s2geography, GDAL and an optional GPU library behind wrapper crates
integration.platforms: PyPI wheels for Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (manylinux_2_28), macOS arm64 and x86-64 (macOS 12+), and Windows x86-64
integration.thread_safety: not documented for the Python/R connection objects; queries run multi-threaded inside the engine
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: SQL with ST_* functions similar to DuckDB Spatial and PostGIS, plus an experimental GeoPandas-compatible API in 0.4.1; not drop-in for any C++ geometry library

gotchas: The join's R-tree stores f32 bounding boxes; exact predicates are evaluated in the refine phase, and which library does that (TG by default, then GEOS or geo) depends on sedona.spatial_join options. TG falls back to geo for predicates it does not support
KNN joins drop tied-distance rows by default (knn_include_tie_breakers = false)
The published SpatialBench numbers are for 0.1.0 with cold reads from S3 and DuckDB's external file cache turned off; later releases have no published re-run on the same hardware
For C/C++ hosts the only native entry point is the ADBC driver (AdbcSedonadbDriverInit in rust/sedona-adbc), which you build from source
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick SedonaDB when the job is a whole spatial query over tables (joins, KNN joins, filters on Parquet) and you are in Python, R or SQL. Use TG or geo-index directly from C or Rust when you only need predicates or an index; SedonaDB uses both inside its join. Arctern targets the same GeoPandas-replacement niche but publishes only its own 24x claim.
verified_claims_summary: Apache Sedona's own SpatialBench (v0.1.0 pre-release, run 2025-09-22) timed SedonaDB 0.1.0, DuckDB 1.4.0 and GeoPandas 1.1.1 with Shapely 2.1.1 on 12 queries at SF1 and SF10, on an AWS m7i.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GB; CPU model not named), from cold S3 Parquet reads, with default settings and no build flags stated. Against DuckDB, SedonaDB was 1.05-1.5x faster on most filter queries, 11x faster on SF1 q10 and 218x/2,480x faster on q9, finished q11-q12 where DuckDB timed out or errored, and was 2.8-3.5x slower on q5 (ratios derived from page data).
status_note: Very active Apache project (509 stars, 1,084 commits, five PyPI releases from 0.1.0 in September 2025 to 0.4.1 on 2026-08-22, main at 0.5.0); Apache-2.0 and pip/conda installable, but it is a Rust engine and not something you vendor into C++.
